summary: Many transport services need pseudowire traffic to be carried over a single co-routed bidirectional tunnel, or over two unidirectional tunnels sharing the same routes. This proposed standard defines an optional extension to LDP that binds a pseudowire to a specific LSP tunnel.

eli5.summary: Imagine telling a delivery truck which exact road to use every time. This lets a network pin a virtual wire to one specific tunnel so its traffic always follows the same path.

subtitle: How two ends of a pseudowire agree, inside LDP signaling, on which tunnel carries the traffic in both directions.

tldr.problem: Each provider edge router picks the tunnel for its own direction of a pseudowire independently, so the two directions can end up on different paths with different latency and protection.
tldr.mechanism: A new optional LDP TLV, the PSN Tunnel Binding TLV, rides in the Label Mapping message and names a tunnel or LSP. A C-bit asks for a co-routed reverse tunnel, and an S-bit demands the named one.
tldr.outcome: Operators get automatic, signaled binding of pseudowires to LSPs instead of manual provisioning, for both single-segment and multi-segment pseudowires.

today: RFC 7965 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself presents the extension as optional.

sections.title: Why Bind Pseudowires to Tunnels
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) emulates a Layer 2 service, such as an Ethernet point-to-point circuit, between two attachment circuits. The emulated traffic is carried between provider edge routers (PEs) over tunnels in a packet switched network (PSN), typically LDP or RSVP-TE label switched paths (LSPs).

The PEs choose and bind pseudowires to tunnels independently. The RFC notes there is no standardized protocol-based way to tie a PW to a tunnel, so such associations are managed by provisioning or private methods.

The RFC's example is two PEs joined by parallel links on different fibers, each managed as a bidirectional LSP. Operators want both pseudowires of a user flow on the same fiber or LSP. Traffic over different fibers may need a large amount of expensive buffer memory to absorb differential delay, and operators may apply different protection schemes, such as 1:1 in one part of the network and 1+1 in another.

Without coordination, PE1 might send over LSP1 while PE2 sends back over LSP2 on a diverse path. The result can be very different latency and protection in each direction. Manual provisioning at each PE is the alternative, but the RFC says it is prone to configuration errors and does not scale.
sections.eli5: If the way there and the way back are different roads, the trip can take very different times. Grown-ups want a way for both ends to agree on one road without writing it down by hand everywhere.

sections.title: The PSN Tunnel Binding TLV
sections.content:
The RFC defines one new optional TLV, the PSN Tunnel Binding TLV, with type 0x0973. It MUST be carried in the LDP Label Mapping message when PW-to-LSP binding is required. Because it is optional, the U-bit MUST be 1 so a receiver that does not know it silently ignores it, and the F-bit MUST be 0 so it is not forwarded further.

After the usual header comes a 2-octet Flags field, a 2-octet Reserved field and one sub-TLV. Three flags are defined, and the rest MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt:

  • C (co-routed): the remote PE SHOULD pick a co-routed LSP for the reverse direction. If none exists, this may trigger it to establish a new LSP.
  • S (strict): the remote PE MUST use the tunnel or LSP named in the sub-TLV for the reverse direction, or the PW fails to be established.
  • T (tunnel representation): when set, the tunnel is identified by tunnel information only and the LSP Number fields MUST be zero. The default is set. The motivation is MPLS protection, where LSP Numbers may be ignored.

Exactly one of C and S MUST be set. If both are set or both are clear, the reply is a Label Release with status "The C-bit or S-bit unknown" (0x0000003C) and the PW is not established.
sections.eli5: The TLV is a note attached to the setup message. A checkbox says either "please use the same road back" or "you must use this exact road".

sections.title: Naming a Tunnel: The PSN Tunnel Sub-TLV
sections.content:
Inside the binding TLV, a PSN Tunnel sub-TLV names the tunnel or LSP. Two exist: the IPv4 sub-TLV (type 1) and the IPv6 sub-TLV (type 2). Each holds a Source Global ID, Source Node ID, Source Tunnel Number and Source LSP Number, followed by the same four fields for the destination.

The identifiers are derived from the MPLS-TP identifiers of RFC 6370, so the LSPs named are globally unique. The ITU-T style identifiers are not used. Following RFC 3209, the Tunnel endpoint address maps to the Destination Node ID and the Extended Tunnel ID maps to the Source Node ID. Node IDs are routable addresses of the ingress and egress LSR.

Each binding TLV MUST carry only one sub-TLV. If a receiver gets more than one, it uses the first and ignores the rest. With the T-bit set, the LSP Number fields MUST be zero and are ignored. Otherwise they MUST hold the actual LSP IDs.
sections.eli5: The sub-TLV is the address of the road: where it starts, where it ends and which lane it is. If you only name the road and not the lane, the lane numbers are left as zero.

sections.title: How Binding Works for Single-Segment PWs
sections.content:
During PW setup, a PE may pick a candidate tunnel or LSP, or trigger a new one if none fits, and send its details in the PSN Tunnel Binding TLV inside the Label Mapping message. The receiver either accepts it or finds a reverse tunnel that meets the request, and answers with its own Label Mapping carrying a binding TLV. Roles come from RFC 6073: the active PE starts the selection and the passive PE obeys it.

For a single-segment PW (SS-PW), both PEs may be active at once, so their choices can collide. The tie-break is to compare Node IDs as unsigned integers. A receiver whose own Node ID is smaller than the received Source Node ID agrees and replies, for strict binding with the same IDs and numbers in the appropriate order. A receiver with the larger Node ID replies with a Label Release and status "Reject - unable to use the suggested tunnel/LSPs" (0x0000003B), and the PW is not established. If the two sides already named the same tunnel, or same-route tunnels in the co-routed case, signaling has converged.

For co-routed binding, the receiver may choose any reverse tunnel with the same links and nodes. For unidirectional LSPs, the sender may fill in only the Source IDs and Numbers and leave Destination fields zero for the peer to complete. If the received tunnel endpoints do not match the PW endpoints, the receiver MUST reject with the same status code.

If a PW is later moved or the tunnel breaks, a new Label Mapping MUST be sent. A new message without the binding TLV removes the co-routed or strict constraint, and ordinary independent binding applies again.
sections.eli5: If both friends suggest a road at the same time, the one with the bigger house number wins, and the other one goes along with it. If they cannot agree, the trip is called off.

sections.title: Binding Across Multi-Segment PWs
sections.content:
A multi-segment PW (MS-PW) is set up with FEC 129 and chains tunnels through switching PEs (S-PEs) between two terminating PEs (T-PEs). Only one end is active here: T-PE1 sends a Label Mapping with the binding TLV to the adjacent S-PE1. For strict binding it sets S and clears C. For co-routed binding it sets C and clears S.

Each S-PE checks whether the message is for the forward or reverse direction, as defined in RFC 7267. In the forward direction, an S-PE that accepts the tunnel saves it for later, picks its own tunnel for the next segment, and relays the message onward with its own sub-TLV. One that cannot accept it replies with a Label Release and status 0x0000003B.

When the message reaches T-PE2 and it agrees, it replies with a Label Mapping that echoes the binding TLV. Each S-PE then relays it back upstream with the information it saved, until T-PE1 receives it and binding is complete. With co-routed binding, a PE may ignore the suggested tunnel for the reverse direction of its segment, but only if its choice is co-routed with the forward one.

If a tunnel changes after setup, the PE that detects it SHOULD pick an alternative for temporary use while it negotiates with the other PEs.
sections.eli5: On a long trip with several stops, each stop writes down which road it was told to use. On the way back, each stop uses what it wrote down, so you come back the same way.

sections.title: Choosing the Kind of Tunnel
sections.content:
The tunnel used for binding can be a co-routed bidirectional LSP or two LSPs with the same route. The RFC points out that a co-routed bidirectional LSP crosses the same nodes and links in both directions and also has the same life span. Two separate LSPs may start on the same route but cannot be guaranteed to stay on it. For example, when Fast ReRoute (RFC 4090) is deployed, a link or node failure may send them different ways.

So if the network supports co-routed bidirectional LSPs, the RFC RECOMMENDS using one. Otherwise, two LSPs with the same route may be used.
sections.eli5: One road with traffic going both ways is safer than two separate roads that only look alike today, because the two roads might get closed at different times.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Being able to control which LSP carries a PW's traffic is a potential security risk, both for denial of service and for traffic interception. The RFC RECOMMENDS that PEs not accept an LSP named in the binding TLV unless its endpoints match the PW or PW segment endpoints. It also RECOMMENDS implementing the LDP security mechanisms of RFC 5036 and the framework in RFC 5920.

IANA assigned TLV type 0x0973, created a PWE3 subregistry called "PSN Tunnel Sub-TLV Name Space" with values 1 (IPv4) and 2 (IPv6), reserved 0 and 255, and left 1 to 254 for IETF Review. Two LDP status codes were added, 0x0000003B and 0x0000003C, both with the E bit set to 1.
sections.eli5: Choosing someone else's road could let a bad actor steal or block their traffic. So a PE should only accept a road that really connects the two ends of the wire.

data.title: PSN Tunnel Binding TLV (header and flags)

fields.name: U
fields.desc: MUST be 1 so unknown receivers silently ignore the TLV.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: MUST be 0 so the TLV is not forwarded.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Octets in the value field, including flags, reserved and sub-TLV.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Strict: named tunnel must be used.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: Tunnel representation; LSP Numbers are zero when set.

fields.name: Unallocated flags
fields.desc: MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt.
